subtopic: Talking with parents about marriage pressure
subtype: Approach: proposing a timeline instead of a flat refusal [Action]
passage: Wednesday, 10 p.m. Raghav, a senior in the hostel, asked me a simple thing today: "What are you asking your parents for, exactly?" I realised I only ever said "no". That's not something they can hold. So tonight I wrote a different offer: let me finish the degree, work for two years, and then we sit down and talk again about marriage. A real date, not a vague someday. I'll tell them Sunday. My hands are already sweating. Raghav says the point is to give them something to hold on to, so they don't feel I am shutting them out. He may be right. If it fails, at least I will have tried it properly. Gautam

qa.q: What is the new offer Gautam wrote for the parents?
qa.a: Gautam wrote to finish the degree, work for two years and then sit down and talk again about marriage.

qa.q: How is Gautam feeling about telling the parents on Sunday?
qa.a: Gautam is nervous, with hands already sweating, but determined to try the offer properly even if it fails.

qa.q: What could Gautam do if the parents ask for a shorter timeline, and why?
qa.a: Gautam could listen to the reason and offer a check-in after one year, because a small step may ease their worry without dropping the plan.

qa.q: How might Gautam's parents see the proposal compared with a flat refusal?
qa.a: Gautam's parents may feel relieved to have a date to look to, because the proposal shows care and gives them something to plan around.

grounding: A young adult proposes finishing a degree and working two years before revisiting marriage instead of refusing outright.
